results.evidence: Only legal rule reference is 'Model Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.4)' — a real, verifiable ABA rule. No bare statute numbers appear anywhere in the post.
No individual attorney or legal expert names appear. Sources cited are institutional only: American Bar Association, Bureau of Justice Statistics.

Two statistics found, both sourced: '#1 bar complaint (American Bar Association)' and 'often 200 or more active cases simultaneously (Bureau of Justice Statistics)'. All other numbers are descriptive or procedural guidance, not factual claims.

Procedural guidance uses expectation framing ('should be in contact within 24-48 hours', 'red flag') rather than legal deadlines. Substitution of counsel qualified with 'typically' and 'judges don't always grant it'. No bare universal procedural claims.
No case citations appear anywhere in the post.

Consequence claims are about attorney discipline from bar complaints ('can result in' reprimand, suspension, disbarment) — properly framed as possibilities. Fee refund qualified with 'likely' and 'may be entitled' and 'depending on'. No unqualified defendant collateral consequences.

results.reason: No question_count field in frontmatter; body contains ~3 direct attorney questions which is reasonable for this format
Major claims cite ABA, Bureau of Justice Statistics, and Model Rules of Professional Conduct Rule 1.4; remaining claims are procedural norms
Action items use plain language with short sentences; legal terms like motion and discovery are contextualized
No instances of banned cliches found; 'nuclear option' is used once but not on the flagged list
Consistent second person 'you/your' throughout; no drift to third person
Predominantly active voice; passive constructions well under 30% threshold
Terms like discovery, motions, arraignment, suppression, substitution of counsel are contextualized on use
Logical flow: problem (silence) -> why -> document -> escalate -> evaluate -> switch/complain -> CTA
Multiple clear CTAs: Case Decoder checkout link, Case Progress Score, and specific micro-actions throughout
Action statements are direct imperatives; hedging mostly appears in information statements which is allowed
All paragraphs well under 300 words; action paragraphs stay under 100 words
Content distributed across ~10 sections with no single section dominating more than 50%
Threats (missed deadlines, trial unprepared, abandonment) are consistently paired with specific actions within 1-2 sentences
Strong opening hook (11 PM scenario), evidence-driven middle (stats, stages, red flags), empowering close with specific CTAs

results.evidence: Post contains multiple direct directives such as 'Send this via email AND certified mail', 'Line up new representation before terminating the old one', and 'Request your complete case file from your current attorney' presented as commands the reader should follow.

Sections discussing firing an attorney, filing a bar complaint, and filing a motion for substitution of counsel contain no proximate redirect to consult an attorney; only a generic footer disclaimer appears at the end.
Post describes general patterns ('signs of effective abandonment') without rendering judgment on the reader's specific legal situation or case strength.

Post recommends specific procedural steps: 'file a motion for substitution of counsel', 'request a copy of your complete case file', and references 'filing a bar complaint' as actions the reader should take.
Post does not discuss immigration consequences, deportation, visa status, or green card issues at all.

Collateral claims like 'Public defenders in some jurisdictions carry very heavy caseloads — often 200 or more active cases' cite only 'Bureau of Justice Statistics' generically without a specific report or URL; ABA attribution is similarly vague.
Post uses only general categories like 'a criminal defense attorney', 'public defender', 'office manager or senior partner' without naming specific firms or companies.
Post avoids 'we recommend/advise/suggest' phrasing in legal-action contexts; uses second-person 'you' framing and 'Consider switching if...' instead.

Opening scenarios like 'It is 11 PM on a Tuesday. You are staring at your phone...' and 'You are sitting across from an empty desk in a law office waiting room' are not labeled as hypothetical or example scenarios.

Phrases like 'You've done the hard part — you showed up, you documented, you educated yourself' and the framing of the reader independently filing bar complaints and case-file requests imply the reader can manage accountability matters themselves.

Rules are stated as certainties without qualifiers: 'A private attorney can be terminated at any time for any reason' and 'The documents in your case file belong to you' appear without 'in general', 'typically', or jurisdictional caveats.

Statement 'A certified letter with a specific deadline is the turning point where most silent attorneys suddenly find time to respond' implies a predictable outcome without qualification that results vary.

The documentation strategy, formal written request template, and accountability questions are presented as the blog's own framework with only vague references to 'Model Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.4)' and no named legal scholar or attorney attribution.
No contradictory legal claims appear; the distinction between private attorneys (terminable at will) and public defenders (requiring court approval) is reconciled explicitly.

Case Decoder is described as the tool 'that turns that effort into results' and 'questions that actually force accountability', framing it as a solution rather than explicitly as a research and preparation tool that does not substitute for legal representation.

Opening TLDR names the documentation fear well, but H2s like 'Why Attorneys Go Silent', 'Know Your Rights as a Client', and 'The Bigger Picture: Communication Problems Are Symptom Problems' are topical rather than action-oriented.

Legal terms defined inline (e.g., 'motion for substitution of counsel (the standard is typically showing a breakdown...)', 'Model Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.4)'), paragraphs stay under 4 sentences, conversational 8th-grade level.
Before the first H2, reader is told: 'open a note on your phone and type today's date and the last time you called. That takes 30 seconds and starts your log.'
Decision points lead with a default (e.g., 'Line up new representation before terminating the old one', 'Send it via email first (for speed) and certified mail second (for proof)').
The 'Why Attorneys Go Silent' section lists 5 unranked reasons, and the numbered action list at top has 7 items without 'start with these' priority labeling.
system-decoder-post — decodes the 'why silent' system, maps behavior to categories (slow vs abandonment), and explains case-stage expectations.

Each threat is paired with action — e.g., '200 or more active cases' is followed by the 'which type are you dealing with' diagnostic, and 'potential malpractice territory' is followed by the switching-attorneys section.
No blame language toward reader; frame is consistently 'your attorney failed you' not 'you should have', e.g., 'You are not a passive bystander in your own defense.'
Arc is present (fear named in opening, clarity in middle, agency in closing), but the final sentence is a CTA ('Take the free Case Progress Score') rather than a pure agency statement.
Communication log table is 6 columns which is borderline, but only H2/H3 used, key actions are bolded, and sections stay in the 300-500 word range.
Every H2 has a bolded standalone sentence under 27 words, e.g., 'A certified letter with a specific deadline is the turning point where most silent attorneys suddenly find time to respond.'
All 3 FAQ answers lead with the direct answer ('Start documenting...', 'Yes.', 'Silence for 1-2 weeks...'), stay in 2-4 sentence range, and read as peer advice rather than institutional voice.
